clinicalPearls: Renin-mediated hypertension caused by external compression of the renal parenchyma, usually by a subcapsular or perinephric haematoma.
It is named after Irvine Page, who reproduced hypertension experimentally by wrapping animal kidneys in cellophane.
Common triggers include trauma (including sporting injury), renal biopsy, anticoagulation, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy, tumour and cysts.
Compression reduces intrarenal perfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in a mechanism analogous to Goldblatt hypertension.
It may present acutely after trauma or a procedure, or as unexplained or resistant hypertension months to years later.
Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI demonstrates the compressing collection and the compressed parenchyma.
Blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is a rational first-line therapy, while acute or refractory cases may need drainage, evacuation or rarely nephrectomy.
Small acute haematomas may resolve spontaneously with improvement in blood pressure.
reference.pathophysiology: Page kidney results from external compression of the kidney by a subcapsular or perinephric collection, most often a haematoma but sometimes a urinoma, tumour or cyst, which raises intraparenchymal pressure and compresses the renal microvasculature. The resulting reduction in renal blood flow is sensed as hypoperfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in a manner analogous to Goldblatt one-kidney hypertension. Angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium retention produce systemic hypertension, which can persist while the compressing lesion and secondary parenchymal ischaemia and fibrosis remain.
additionalDifferentials: Renovascular hypertension from renal artery stenosis
Renal artery or vein thrombosis after trauma
Acute kidney injury of another cause after trauma or a procedure
additionalInvestigations: Contrast CT or MRI of the kidneys showing the compressing collection and compressed parenchyma
Blood pressure profiling or ambulatory monitoring
Coagulation screen if anticoagulated or with spontaneous haematoma
Isotope renography for differential function where intervention is considered
redFlags: Severe or accelerated hypertension with end-organ damage
An underlying malignancy as the compressing lesion
reference.prognosis: The outlook is often good, with hypertension resolving as an acute haematoma reabsorbs or after drainage or evacuation; chronic compression with established parenchymal fibrosis may cause persistent hypertension requiring long-term therapy or intervention.
pitfalls: Overlooking Page kidney as a reversible cause of secondary or resistant hypertension after trauma, biopsy or lithotripsy
Attributing post-procedural hypertension to essential hypertension
Premature nephrectomy when drainage or medical therapy would suffice
Failing to recognise a malignant compressing lesion
management: Control the renin-angiotensin-driven hypertension pharmacologically, using an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker to target the activated pathway
Manage an acute subcapsular haematoma conservatively where possible, allowing reabsorption with blood-pressure control and analgesia, and reverse or withhold anticoagulation
Evacuate or drain the compressing collection, or undertake surgical decompression or capsulectomy, when hypertension is severe or persistent
Reserve nephrectomy for a non-functioning kidney with refractory hypertension after other measures fail
Monitor blood pressure including ambulatory profiling, renal function, and the collection on serial cross-sectional imaging
Refer to nephrology and urology, escalating for uncontrolled or resistant hypertension or deteriorating renal function
